segments.t: Now Andréa walks straight to the assistants' desks, where Camille is working next to Hervé and Noémie. You'll hear the whole scene in French first. Don't worry about catching every word; we'll go through it together afterwards. Let's listen to the scene in French first.
Pas de chance pour moi!
Je trouve une assistante qui me plaît.
Mais je me suis trompée.
Tu réalises ce que tu as fait?
Tu voulais un selfie? Un autographe?
Nous avons presque perdu une grande star!
Oui, mais Cécile est restée à l'agence.
Non, ce n'est pas comme ça.
Je ne suis pas bavarde.
Prends tes affaires.
C'était bref, mais intense.
Mais il y a un côté positif.
Tu es loin de ce business. Je le pense vraiment.
Noémie, dis au revoir à Camille!
Ce n'est pas grave. Elle est pressée.
Bon, au revoir.
Au revoir, Camille. Bon courage!
Je suis sûre qu'on se reverra.
Let's take it from the top. Andréa doesn't shout straight away; she starts with a sigh, as if the bad luck were all hers.
Pas de chance pour moi!
'Unlucky me!' Literally 'no luck for me'. It's sarcastic: Camille is the one about to be in trouble. Then Andréa explains.
Je trouve une assistante qui me plaît.
'I find an assistant I like.' Word for word, 'an assistant who pleases me'. That's how French says 'I like her': the person does the pleasing. And then the twist.
Mais je me suis trompée.

'But I was wrong.' Listen to the ending of the last word. Andréa is a woman, so the word gets a silent extra letter, the feminine ending. You won't hear it, but you'll see it written. Now she turns on Camille.
Tu réalises ce que tu as fait?
'Do you realise what you did?' Andréa uses the casual 'you' with her assistant. A boss can do that, and in this office everyone does. Then she mocks her.
Tu voulais un selfie? Un autographe?
'Did you want a selfie? An autograph?' Andréa pretends Camille only talked to the star to get a souvenir, like a fan. Then comes the serious part.
Nous avons presque perdu une grande star!
'We almost lost a big star!' The word for 'almost' sits between the two parts of the verb, just like 'we have almost lost'. Camille tries to defend herself.
Oui, mais Cécile est restée à l'agence.
'Yes, but Cécile stayed with the agency.' True: Mathias got her to sign with him, so she's still a client of the house. Then Camille says it didn't happen that way.
Non, ce n'est pas comme ça.

'No, it isn't like that.' Here's the main grammar point of this scene. To say 'not', French wraps the verb in two little words, one before and one after. The first one loses its vowel before 'is'. Listen to it again in the next line.
Je ne suis pas bavarde.

'I'm not a chatterbox.' Same pattern: the two little negative words hug the verb 'am'. The word for 'chatterbox' ends in the feminine form, because Camille is talking about herself. Andréa doesn't want to hear it.
Prends tes affaires.
'Get your things.' Three words, and Camille is fired. It's a casual command, said to one person. Hervé, at the next desk, tries to soften the blow.
C'était bref, mais intense.
'It was short, but intense.' Notice how 'it was' sets up the clause and leads naturally into 'intense'.
Mais il y a un côté positif.
'But there's a bright side.' Literally 'there is a positive side'. The opening three words mean 'there is', and you hear them everywhere in French.
Tu es loin de ce business.
'You're far from this business.' Hervé means she has escaped a nasty world. The word for business is simply the English one.
Je le pense vraiment.
'I really mean it.' Literally 'I think it really'. Now Hervé turns to Noémie, who hasn't looked up from her screen.
Noémie, dis au revoir à Camille!
'Noémie, say goodbye to Camille!' Another casual command, from the verb 'to say'. Noémie mumbles that she's too busy, and Camille covers for her.
Ce n'est pas grave.
'It doesn't matter.' Literally 'it isn't serious', with the same two negative words around the verb. It's what French people say all day long when something is no big deal.
Elle est pressée.
'She's in a hurry.' One more feminine ending: Noémie is a woman, so the adjective takes the extra letter. Camille picks up her bag.
Bon, au revoir.
'Well, goodbye.' The first word is a little sigh that means 'right then'. Hervé answers warmly.
Au revoir, Camille. Bon courage!
'Goodbye, Camille. Good luck!' The second phrase literally means 'good courage', and it's how you wish someone strength for something hard. And Camille leaves on a hopeful note.
Je suis sûre qu'on se reverra.

'I'm sure we'll see each other again.' The word for 'sure' is in the feminine again. She doesn't know it yet, but she's right. Now listen to the whole scene once more, and see how much of it you can follow.
Pas de chance pour moi!
Je trouve une assistante qui me plaît.
Mais je me suis trompée.
Tu réalises ce que tu as fait?
Tu voulais un selfie? Un autographe?
Nous avons presque perdu une grande star!
Oui, mais Cécile est restée à l'agence.
Non, ce n'est pas comme ça.
Je ne suis pas bavarde.
Prends tes affaires.
C'était bref, mais intense.
Mais il y a un côté positif.
Tu es loin de ce business. Je le pense vraiment.
Noémie, dis au revoir à Camille!
Ce n'est pas grave. Elle est pressée.
Bon, au revoir.
Au revoir, Camille. Bon courage!
Je suis sûre qu'on se reverra.
That's the end of a very short first job. If you picked up the two little words that wrap around a verb to make it negative, you've learned something you'll use every single day. Until next time.
Au revoir!
